games.explanation: Yamamoto is a legitimate ace, but a plus-money dog gets interesting when the park does half the work and the lineup finally has a lefty-heavy setup pitching against its strengths. Cincinnati's ballpark plays like a launching pad in the heat, and Yamamoto has been noticeably more hittable against righties, where his barrel rate against nearly triples what lefties manage off him. Elly and Sal Stewart are exactly the kind of right-handed thump that can turn a well-pitched game into a one-swing loss, and the Reds only need to scratch out four or five to make this a live coin flip. At +205 on a night where the ball carries and the underdog projects within a run, the price is doing the arguing.

Sanchez is one of those lefties whose overall numbers look scarier than the specific problem he's about to face, because Washington rolls out a lineup that skews right-handed and doesn't particularly care about a changeup-heavy arm. The splits are the whole story here: Sanchez has been ordinary against righties this year while dominating the few lefties he sees, and James Wood at the top of the order is exactly the kind of bat that turns an ordinary start into a bad one. The sim has this as a one-run game, which is what you'd expect when the better team's pitching edge gets neutralized by handedness. At +182 on a projected 4.5 to 4.8 final, the board is charging you full price for a matchup that quietly isn't there.

Hunter Brown is priced like an ace against a lineup the market has already written off, but the Royals actually run out a top four that can hurt him. Bobby Witt and Salvador Perez have been mashing right-handed pitching all year, and Carter Jensen has been quietly turning in the loudest contact on the roster in his small look. This is a coin-flip game between two teams the ratings can't separate, played in a neutral park with the roof shut, and Kansas City is getting paid like the clear underdog. +140 on a game the numbers call a virtual toss-up is the entire argument.

Gilbert's surface line looks like an ace, but the peripherals against right-handed bats are noticeably softer than the reputation, and the Angels happen to run their thump from that side. Neto and Trout have both been barreling righties at rates that travel, and a fly-ball park with the wind doing nothing to help the pitcher is not where you want a homer-prone starter working. Seattle is the better team, sure, but the sim has this within a run and the market is pricing it like a mismatch. At +148 on a game projected inside a field goal, you're getting paid to take the side the board forgot to look twice at.

Griffin Jax is a nasty right-handed reliever being asked to do a starter's job, and the split that matters is the one the market is ignoring: lefties have handled him just fine. The Athletics can run a lineup full of them at him, and once he's out of the game you're into a Rays bullpen that isn't built to hold a two-run lead across four innings. The sim sees this as a one-run game, essentially a coin flip disguised as a mismatch, and the projected margin lands inside a tenth of a run. Getting a run and a half at a plus-adjacent price on a game that projects to end 4-3 is the entire ballgame.

Washington gets shorter than the price suggests any time a low-scoring script is on the menu, and Cristopher Sánchez is exactly the pitcher who writes one. The Nats send a lefty-heavy top of the order at a southpaw who has been notably more human against right-handed bats, and James Wood in particular has the kind of profile that doesn't care which arm slot shows up. Even the projected final lands inside a run, which is the whole reason a plus-money hook exists. Getting +105 on the underdog plus the run in a game the sim sees as a coin flip is how you print tickets against public chalk.

The Yankees are the better team and Fried is the better pitcher, but a run and a half is a lot of cushion in a game the simulator has landing inside a field goal. Wind blowing in on a mild night takes the Judge nuke off the table just enough to matter, and Ober has quietly been the kind of arm who gives up loud contact without giving up crooked innings. Minnesota's right-handed core, Bell in particular against righties, matches up fine with Fried, whose numbers versus RHB are noticeably more human than his headline line suggests. Our number lands on a projected margin of roughly a third of a run, which is nowhere near the run and a half you're getting back. At -111, you're buying the pushes and the backdoors and letting the Bronx do whatever it wants in the ninth.

Seattle should be favored here, but a run and a half is a lot to lay in a game the sims see decided by a single run. Gilbert is excellent, though the platoon split cuts the other way this year, and Neto and Trout are the exact right-handed profiles that punish him when he misses. Ryan Johnson's small-sample ERA looks ugly, but the underlying contact quality he's allowed is closer to average than disastrous, and a wind blowing straight in should shrink the margin for error on both sides. At -110, you're getting a coin flip on whether this stays a one-run game, and the math says it usually does.
